en: Shi Zhao’s preface states that the *Ben-shen* (Original Depth) is profound. "Qi" means to open. It is like the worldly opening of what is deep, which cannot be done without the royal seal;
this is the metaphor. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra*...
The Sūtra says:
"This treasury of the Lotus Sūtra is profound, firm, and remote; no one can reach it.
Its words and phrases are quiescent."
This sutra states:
"The characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) are thus; how could they be expressed in words?
This can only be realized through wisdom.
As for the objection that the manifestations of the Sage should not differ:
this is because the traces [of his response] are distinct,
as sentient beings' perceptions vary.
The Dharma-Buddha and the Responsive Buddha must be distinct.
Since the Buddha-body manifests according to the response of sentient beings, it consequently appears in a thousand different ways; therefore, they are said to be "not the same.

This collectively indicates that both the fundamental and the manifested traces are inconceivable. "Without the fundamental, there would be no way to manifest the traces; without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental."
Thus, if the Sage did not abide in the fundamental principle of non-duality,
there would be no way to manifest the myriad distinct traces;
and if sentient beings did not encounter these myriad distinct traces, [they could not attain liberation].
There is no means by which to awaken to the fundamental source of non-duality.
Thus, Master Zhao said:
"The cause is not used to demonstrate the root."
To rely on the coarse to manifest the subtle is precisely what this refers to.
Tiantai’s discernment of the fundamental and the trace consists briefly of five layers.
First, the true and the conventional;
second, principle and teaching;
third, principle and practice.

The four aspects of essence and function, and the five aspects of provisional and real, are all instances of manifesting traces based on the fundamental source; by seeking these traces, one finds the source. Although the source and the traces differ, they are inconceivably one.
Because the fundamental and the manifested depend upon one another, they are explained together.
Thus, a poem says:
"In the south there is a drooping tree; the climbing vine entwines it."
The lower bowl is called *jiū*;
the upper bowl is called *jù*.
It is like blowing upon a lofty pine tree, its substance reaching out into the heights of the clouds.
When the kudzu vine spreads and entangles itself beneath the thorny brush,
the vine, despite its power of climbing, remains no higher than the weeds and brambles.
If the drooping branches of a tree do not provide a connection for the vine to grasp and climb upward, it cannot ascend.
Thus, even a tree a thousand fathoms tall may find a way to reach the top by relying on others;
the principle of the Dharma is likewise.
Yet, if the Tathāgata dwells above the nine heavens while sentient beings sink below the three miserable realms, there can be no mutual resonance or meeting between them.
Thus, although all living beings possess the wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛtistha-gotra*),
they cannot avoid the suffering of saṃsāra; yet,
if the common people were to cultivate a profound sincerity of faith, [they would be liberated].
When the Buddhas manifest the traces of their great compassion,
then even though the stage of the Ten Powers is exalted and the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are distant,
all may achieve success through unremitting self-exertion.
The meaning of the "Original and the Traces" is thus made manifest.
This is the third section, clarifying the title of the work;
therefore, he commanded his attendant to record it by name.
In the "Chapter on Entrustment," the Buddha told Ānanda, "This sutra is named 'The Teaching of Vimalakīrti,' and it is also named 'The Dharma Gate of Inconceivable Liberation.
He then commanded Ānanda to serve as his attendant."
This is because both the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku) are inconceivable;
thus, "Inconceivable" is adopted as the title.
Third, this explains the reason for the retranslation.
This is a retranslation because the previous translation lost its original intent.
The text consists of four parts;
the first clarifies the master who translated the scripture.
This refers to Yao Xing, the ruler of the Qin dynasty.
As for the second point regarding the time of the translation of the scriptures,
it was the eighth year of the Hongshi era.
Third, the person who was able to translate:
Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
Fourth, the Dharma that was translated.
This is precisely that sutra.
The preceding text consists of two parts;
the first introduces the person and extols their virtues.
Second, explaining the original intent of the retranslation.
First, "the Great Qin Heavenly King" refers to the person;
"the divine spirit," etc., praises his virtue.
The people of Da Qin (the Roman Empire) extol their Great King;
the king honors those individuals who are noble,
and because his sagely virtue covers all universally, they call him "Heaven."
The common people looked up to him with devotion and followed him, calling him "King.
This was the virtue of governing through filial piety; hence the *Classic of Filial Piety* says:
"In ancient times, the enlightened kings governed the world through filial piety."

They did not dare to neglect even the subjects of the small states, let alone those of the dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons; thus they won the affection of the myriad states and could be sustained by the people, which is what is meant by being "Heaven."
Among humans, one who possesses mastery is called a "king";
this is a title for the most honored.
A "divine spirit" (shen) refers to one who is brilliant and also one who is eminent.
There is an interpretation:
those who have recently surpassed ten people are called *hao* (豪);
those who surpass a hundred are called *ying* (英).
Among a thousand people, one is called a "talent" (jun);
among ten thousand people, one is called a "prodigy" (jie).
"Spiritual" (shen) refers to spiritual thought.
This refers to those with extraordinary minds, such as the "Eminent Men of the World" (shìyīng).
Therefore, it is said they "transcend the world.
This praises the wisdom of governing a state; it refers to those whose profound minds attain solitary awakening.
Because the mind roams within the profound mirror, it is called the "profound mind" (xuánxīn).
Because its subtle discernment is peerless, it is named "solitary awakening" (dúwù).
This praises the mind that awakens to principle. To propagate the ultimate truth amidst the myriad affairs of governance— [End of excerpt]
"Hong" (弘) means great, as it extends its imperial edicts to the myriad regions; thus it is called "great.
"Zhi" (至) means ultimate. As for "governing and transforming the myriad affairs," it refers to the management of all state functions.
The pivot of all affairs is subtle.
The Book of Documents says:
"With utmost vigilance and earnestness, in one day and two days there are ten thousand pivots."

Herein lies the account of how the King of Qin excelled in governing the state, so that while he sat with his robes trailing and his hands clasped in formal ease, all things naturally submitted to him.

Although he occupied himself with the myriad affairs of state, he did not lose the transformative power of the heavenly mandate—thus propagating the Way and its transformation for a thousand years to come.
"Yang" means to propagate;
"hua" refers to the transformation through the Dharma.
"Qianzai" (a thousand ages) refers to years.
More than one thousand three hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
the supreme teachings of the Mahāyāna were finally transmitted to this land.
Because the Ruler of Qin responded to this pivotal destiny, he was able to extensively honor and propagate the Dharma transformation.
Thus, because he transcended worldly affairs through his numinous spirit, he was able to propagate the ultimate truth amidst the myriad affairs of state.
Because his profound mind attained solitary awakening, he was able to exalt the transformation of the Way for a thousand years.
Since he preceded these myriad affairs, he is called "Supreme" (Shang).
Because it was produced a thousand years later, it is called "the latter" (xia).
From this point, the second section clarifies the purpose of the re-translation.
Whenever one seeks out and contemplates this scripture, it serves as the dwelling place for the spirit; those who seek out, contemplate, and practice it do so for this very reason.
"Canon" (diǎn) refers to the scriptures;
"by means of" (yǐ) means to employ;
"to act" (wéi) means to create.
"To dwell" (*xi*) means to come to rest.
It is the place where the spirit abides.
What follows below explains that "ultimate emptiness and stillness" is the causal meaning of a "dwelling."
This clarifies that the Lord of Qin obtained ancient translations of the sūtras and frequently consulted them;
it was also [the place] where he refined those works produced by Parśva, Zhi Qian, and Dharmarakṣa whose principles were obstructed by their phrasing.
"Zhi" refers to Zhi Qian;
"Zhu" refers to Dharmarakṣa.
The principle was obstructed by [the following]: in a sūtra translated by Zhi Qian, the phrase "coming with the characteristic of non-coming" was rendered as "coming as an insult."
"Not seeing marks while seeing them as marks" and so forth—this is the Mahāyāna principle being hindered by the phrasing of the translator. Why is this?
As in the translations by Kumārajīva:
The Sūtra says: "He comes without the appearance of coming; he is seen without the appearance of being seen.
This is refined in its adherence to the ultimate principle and does not lose the meaning of responsive harmony.
To speak of "honoring yourself by coming to see me" involves the mundane and the superficial.
As for the Way of awakening to principle, it is entirely beyond [sensory] form, as worldly people say of those they have not met face-to-face.
In the past, you humbled yourself to come and see me;

could a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body truly meet with others by grasping at conventional appearances? I have always feared that the profound essence of the teaching might fall into error through the translators.
Since the translations have already deviated from the intent of the scriptures,
I fear that the profound and subtle essence of the teaching may fall into the hands of the translators.
As for the destiny of the Northern Heaven, there is one whose fortune is currently aligned with it.
"Northern Heaven" refers to the country of North India.
"Yun" (運) means movement or turning.
As it says in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
The Buddha clearly prophesied that after his parinirvāṇa, this sutra would be transmitted to Southern India,
then to Western India,
and finally to Northern India.
When it disappears into the earth,

according to the calculation of its movement, it will remain in the southern heavens for five hundred years and in the western heavens for five hundred years before finally reaching the northern heavens.
This country is none other than Northern India.
Because it lies at the eastern corner of the land,
after a thousand years, the Great Teaching shall be transmitted together here.
Because the Buddha spoke of the fruit, it is said that there is pervasiveness throughout existence.
Second, clarifying the time of the translation: "The eighth year of Hongshi, the year-cycle being Chunchu (the Fire Bird)," means the Tai-sui was in the position of Wu;
this should be called Dunxiang.
When the moon is in the fifth lunar mansion, it is called "Cranes' Fire" (Chunhuo).
This is because the year is designated by the name of the month;
this is from the *Erya*. As for the appointment of the Great General, Duke Changshan: [text continues].
Yao Song was the Marquis of Ancheng; Yao Xian was also [the Marquis of Ancheng].
Changshan and Ancheng were the fiefs to which they were enfeoffed.
"Gong" refers to the five grades of feudal lords: gong, hou, bo, zi, and nan;
this is simply citing the titles of those enfeoffed. "At the Great Temple in Chang'an":
the Qin ruler's taboo name was Chang.
Because he was the son of Yao Chang, his name is Chang.
This is the site where the scriptures were translated;
it is a separate location within the Great Monastery.
As for Cao Tang Si (Grass Hall Monastery), it was called "Cao Tang" because the hall was thatched with grass;
the assembly of monks there was referred to as a "Great Monastery.
These were all contemporary designations rather than original names. Regarding those who associated with śramaṇas specializing in the study of meaning (yìxué):
Those who grasp the correct principles distinguish themselves from other students;
indeed, Sengzhao, Daosheng, Tanrong, Fayun, Huiyuan, Huiguan, and others—numbering one thousand two hundred—were all the preeminent talents of their time.
The various significant deeds and the journey to the West,
as well as the matter of requesting Master Kumārajīva to translate the scriptures and so forth, are detailed in the *Chao* (Excerpts) and the biographies (*zhuan*).
Thirdly, from this point, we shall clarify the translators.
This is divided into two parts:
first, citing the person and praising their virtue; second, clarifying the purpose of translating the scriptures.
Regarding the first part, citing the person by the name "Master Shi": "With a capacity that transcends the world," and so forth.
This is an exaltation of his virtues.
It is said that because his wisdom and capacity are lofty and far-reaching, they transcend the world.
"To cause the mind to merge with the true realm" means that the mind and the principle are in profound accord. "Having exhausted the center of the circle" means...
When wisdom exhausts the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
it is as Zhuangzi said:
"Grasp the beginning and find its pivot in the center to respond to the infinite."
They take "is" and "is not" to be a cycle;
this state where "is" and "is not" are severed is the center of the circle.
Now, I borrow their words to clarify the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, one who is skilled in local dialects [understands that]...
He was well-versed in the dialects of both India and China.
This is the second point regarding his intention for translating the scriptures: at that time, he held the Indic manuscripts in his hands while reciting the translations himself.
"Indic manuscripts" refers to the Sanskrit texts.
This means that those who claim to have inherited the remaining teachings of Brahmā are in error regarding the words and phrases.
Thus, the venerable master of Nanshan said:
"These are still but pebbles from Mount Kunlun."
Since Dharma Master Kumārajīva was proficient in the languages of both countries, he translated orally himself.
As for those among the clergy and laity who were reverent:
"clergy" refers to śramaṇas who study the meaning of the teachings.
In common parlance, they are called "patriarchs of Confucianism" and "masters of rhetoric.
These are all individuals who have realized the meaning of the teachings through personal verification.
As for those who are reverent:
"Qian" (虔) means reverence. To speak twice expresses a will of sincere reverence; to "repeat three times" refers to re-examining and confirming the meaning of the words.
Thus, in the *Analects*, it is said that the Southern Guest repeated [the line] "White jade may be chipped," hence the saying: "The flaws on white jade can still be polished away."
These words cannot be considered superficial;
therefore, whenever one reads the *Shijing* to this point, one always recites them three times.
Now, I have merely cited those words here.
That is to say, the text elucidates correct principles and serves as a guide for regulating things;
when the mind grasps its essential meaning, the fruits of the Path are thereby accomplished,
whereas if one loses that intent, various false views arise from it.

Therefore, one must read it three times over. Those who refine and seek with precision to preserve the sagely intent take "clay" (táo) to mean "to knead earth," and "furnace" (yě) to mean "to smelt metal."
This is an analogy.
It is like a potter who sifts and removes sand and saline soil from the clay,
or like a goldsmith who melts and casts metal to extract only its pure essence.
Thus, one is able to complete its functional utility.
Now it is the same here: by eliminating redundant words and directly explicating the Sage’s intent, the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure is completed.
This clarifies the purpose of translating the scriptures.
Regarding this fourth Dharma translated from hereon: its text is concise yet reaches its ultimate meaning, and its purport is elegant yet manifest.
"Concise" means abbreviated;
"reaches" means to arrive at.
Although these explicit explanations are concise and brief, their principle reaches the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The meaning is that while the intent is subtle, it is also manifest;
"subtle" here signifies being compliant and harmonious.
This clarifies and elucidates [the meaning].
For example, in verses such as those from the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (The Mother of the Bodhisattvas),
the intent is elegant and conforms to principle.
Furthermore, this further clarifies the preceding preface:
it explains that because the ancients had not yet fully integrated the grand perspective, their principles were stunted and incomplete;
and because they were constrained by local dialects, their expressions were coarse.
Now, because Master Kumārajīva has fully realized the center within the circle, his purport is subtle yet manifest;
because he was skilled in local dialects, his prose is concise yet reaches its destination; thus, words that were previously obscure and distant have become clearly evident here.
"Subtle" (*wei*) means profound and subtle. Laozi said:
"Grasp it and you cannot get hold of it; this is called the subtle."
"Far-reaching" means profound and far-reaching.
"Manifestly clear" means luminous.
This clarifies the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Although it is profound, firm, obscure, and remote,
through translation its essential meaning is attained, thereby making it manifest;
this is the attainment of the intended meaning in this translation and transmission.
From this fourth section, the purpose of providing commentary is clarified.
Although the principles are easy to perceive once the translation is clear,
there remains a fear that they may still be difficult to comprehend for those who have not yet attained realization.
Therefore, it is necessary to provide annotations to enlighten future students.
The text has two parts.
First, the expression of humility.
Second, clarifying the attention. Regarding the first part: "I, who am short-sighted and ignorant"—here, "I" refers to myself.
"As" means "regarding.
"Ignorant" refers to delusion and darkness.
"Short" means brief or shallow. "Participating in the listening" refers to taking part in it.
This was at the time when Dharma Master Kumārajīva was translating the scriptures.
Regarding the phrase "he attended the lectures," Sengzhao personally received the Master’s oral teachings;

hence it is said that he was "present at the time of the lecture. Although his reflections lacked the depth to penetrate the profound mysteries—"reflection" here refers to intellectual contemplation—[the text continues].
"Pai" (乏) means "few.
"San" (參) means "to traverse.
"Xuan" (玄) refers to the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This means that because the mind has not awakened to the principle, it is said thus.

However, those who have a coarse grasp of the meaning of the text, though their words may not be refined or profound, at least roughly understand the ultimate aim. Thus, I have hastily provided these annotations in accordance with what I have heard.
"Zhuē" (辄) means to act independently.
"Wéi" (为) means to create.
This is a brief record of established words, recounted rather than composed.
"Jì" (ji) means recording.
There are two types of sincere speech;
sometimes it is written as "chéng" (chéng).
This sūtra is established.
The word "sūtra" (jing) is sometimes written as "cheng" (zheng).
"Cheng" means reality or what is appropriate.
This records the Master Kumārajīva’s sincere and appropriate words for the purpose of explaining this sutra:
"To transmit without creating; as the *Lunyu* says, 'Transmitting without creating, trusting and loving antiquity.'"
I clarify that it is only the sages who compose such works; I merely recount the words of the ancients and do not dare to compose anything myself.
Second, I clarify the intent behind these annotations, hoping that gentlemen of the future, though separated by different eras, may share in this same understanding.
"Shu" (庶) expresses hope.
"Jianglai" (將來) refers to the future.
The gentleman distinguishes himself from the small man.
Laozi said:
"The superior man, upon hearing the Way, practices it with diligence;
the mediocre man, upon hearing the Way, is as if it exists and as if it does not."
The inferior man hears the Way and laughs at it in derision.
Since the petty person is unable to practice and uphold it,
the text speaks only of the "gentleman" (junzi).
These words need not be taken as a dismissal of one's intention;
they are intended merely to encourage and inspire self-exertion.

It is said because those who hear this together, though in different lifetimes, will experience no difference in their realization or the benefits gained from hearing the sutras and attaining awakening, whether in the present life or in future times when the world has become more mundane.
In the first month of the spring of the second year of the Dali era, while transmitting the scriptures at Zisheng Monastery, I recorded what I had heard to remedy my many lapses of memory.
It is my hope that future readers will understand the meaning and not reproach me for this somewhat florid composition.
The Record of the Monk Tǐqǐng of Chóngfú Monastery, with the Preface by Shì Zhào, is briefly divided into four parts:

First, a general discussion of the fundamental and the manifested; this is divided into two: First, designating the title and offering a general eulogy; Second, explaining the teachings through successive dharmas. Second, a general demonstration of the merit and benefit;

this is divided into two: First, explaining false conceptualization; Second, summarizing to demonstrate its error. Second, specifically analyzing the arising of the teachings; this is divided into two.
III. First, the assembly of those who jointly propagated [the teaching]; second, clarifying the teaching that was propagated, which is divided into three parts:

first, clarifying the inconceivability of the fundamental; second, clarifying the inconceivability of the manifested traces; third, clarifying the inconceivability of the unity of the fundamental and the manifested traces.

III. Third, clarifying the title of the sutra, which is divided into four parts: first, clarifying the master who translated the sutra, which is further divided into two parts: first, citing the person and praising their virtues; second, clarifying...

The meaning of the "Re-translated" [Preface] is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the time of the translation of the sutras; second, clarifying the person who performed the translation. This is further divided into two: first, citing the person and praising their virtue;
second, the purpose of translating the sutras. Fourth, clarifying the dharma that was translated. Fourth, manifesting the reason for the commentary, which is divided into two:
first, expressing modesty; second, clarifying the intent of the notes.
